topics.name: Next.js
topics.description: React framework for production — routing, SSR, SSG, and more

questions.question: What is the default rendering strategy in Next.js App Router?
questions.explanation: App Router defaults to Static Site Generation — components are rendered at build time unless you opt into dynamic rendering.

questions.question: Which file defines the root layout in the Next.js App Router?
questions.explanation: app/layout.tsx is the required root layout that wraps all pages in the App Router.

questions.question: How do you create a dynamic route segment in the App Router?
questions.explanation: Square brackets like [slug] create a dynamic segment. In the App Router it must be a folder, e.g. app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx.

questions.question: What does the 'use client' directive do?
options: Marks the component as a Client Component
Makes the component run only on the server
questions.explanation: 'use client' marks the boundary where React's client-side features (useState, useEffect, event handlers) are used.

questions.question: Which Next.js function fetches data at request time (SSR) in the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: getServerSideProps runs on every request, enabling Server-Side Rendering for that page.

questions.question: What is ISR in Next.js?
questions.explanation: ISR lets you update static pages after build time by specifying a revalidate interval in getStaticProps.

questions.question: Which option in getStaticProps enables ISR?
questions.explanation: Returning { revalidate: N } from getStaticProps tells Next.js to regenerate the page at most every N seconds.

questions.question: Where do you place API route handlers in the Pages Router?
questions.explanation: Files under pages/api/ automatically become serverless API endpoints.

questions.question: In the App Router, which HTTP methods does a route.ts file export to handle requests?
options: Named exports: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.
questions.explanation: App Router route handlers export named functions matching HTTP methods: GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE, etc.

questions.question: What is the purpose of next/image?
options: Provides automatic image optimisation, lazy loading and responsive sizes
questions.explanation: next/image automatically optimises images (size, format, lazy-load) and is served via Next.js's built-in image API.

questions.question: Which component should you use for client-side navigation in Next.js?
questions.explanation: next/link's <Link> component provides client-side transitions, prefetching, and is the recommended navigation method.

questions.question: What does next/font do?
options: Embeds Google Fonts via a CDN
Downloads fonts at build time and self-hosts them for zero layout shift
questions.explanation: next/font downloads fonts at build time, eliminates external network requests, and has zero CLS by design.

questions.question: How do you run a Next.js development server?
questions.explanation: next dev starts the local development server with Hot Module Replacement on port 3000 by default.

questions.question: What does next build produce?
questions.explanation: next build compiles and optimises the app into the .next folder containing static assets and server bundles.

questions.question: What is Middleware in Next.js?
options: Code that runs before a request is processed, at the Edge
questions.explanation: Middleware runs at the Edge before requests hit the server, enabling redirects, rewrites, auth checks, etc.

questions.question: Which file defines Middleware in Next.js?
questions.explanation: middleware.ts (or .js) must be placed at the root of the project (alongside /app or /pages).

questions.question: What is a React Server Component (RSC)?
options: A component that only runs in the browser
A component rendered on the server with no client-side JS bundle
A component in a separate server process
questions.explanation: RSCs are rendered exclusively on the server; their code never ships to the client, reducing bundle size.

questions.question: Can React Server Components use useState or useEffect?
options: No, they must be Client Components for hooks
Only with a special server version
questions.explanation: useState, useEffect, and other client-only APIs require 'use client'. RSCs cannot use them.

questions.question: What is a Parallel Route in Next.js App Router?
options: Multiple pages sharing the same URL
Simultaneously rendering multiple pages in the same layout using @folder slots
A redirect to two routes at once
A route that handles multiple HTTP methods
questions.explanation: Parallel Routes use @folder convention to render multiple independent pages within the same layout simultaneously.

questions.question: What is an Intercepting Route used for?
options: Loading a route within the current layout while keeping the URL structure (e.g. a modal)
questions.explanation: Intercepting Routes (using (.) syntax) let you open a route — like a photo in a modal — without leaving the current context.

questions.question: How do you enable Static Exports in Next.js?
options: Both A and B in older versions
questions.explanation: Since Next.js 13.3+, set output: 'export' in next.config.js. The legacy next export command is deprecated.

questions.question: What does the revalidatePath() function do in Server Actions?
options: Clears a specific path from the router cache
Sets the ISR revalidation time for a path
Forces a hard reload of the page
questions.explanation: revalidatePath() purges the cached data for a specific path, triggering a fresh fetch on the next request.

questions.question: What are Server Actions in Next.js?
options: Async functions that run on the server, invoked directly from Client Components
questions.explanation: Server Actions (marked 'use server') let you define server-side mutations that Client Components can call like regular functions.

questions.question: Which Next.js hook returns the current pathname in the App Router?
questions.explanation: usePathname() from 'next/navigation' returns the current URL pathname in App Router components.

questions.question: How do you programmatically navigate in the App Router?
questions.explanation: import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation'; then call router.push('/path') for client-side navigation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of loading.tsx in App Router?
options: Shows a loading UI automatically while the page segment is fetching
Wraps the page in a Suspense boundary only on mobile
questions.explanation: loading.tsx wraps the page.tsx segment in a Suspense boundary, showing the loading UI during data fetching.

questions.question: What file handles 404 pages in the App Router?
questions.explanation: not-found.tsx is rendered when notFound() is called or when no route matches.

questions.question: What is error.tsx used for in App Router?
options: Segment-level error boundary that catches runtime errors in that subtree
questions.explanation: error.tsx creates an error boundary for the route segment. It must be a Client Component to use reset().

questions.question: How does Next.js handle environment variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_?
options: They are injected at build time and exposed to the browser
questions.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix tells Next.js to inline the variable into the client bundle, making it accessible in the browser.

questions.question: What is the Turbopack bundler?
options: Vercel's Rust-based bundler replacing webpack for faster builds
questions.explanation: Turbopack is an incremental Rust-based bundler designed to be significantly faster than webpack, integrated into Next.js.

questions.question: What does the next.config.js file configure?
options: Build behaviour, redirects, rewrites, environment variables, custom headers, and more
questions.explanation: next.config.js is the central configuration for the Next.js build pipeline, routing rules, images, and experimental features.

questions.question: How do you set up a redirect in Next.js?
options: In the redirects() function in next.config.js
questions.explanation: next.config.js exports an async redirects() function returning an array of { source, destination, permanent } objects.

questions.question: What is the Pages Router equivalent of loading.tsx?
questions.explanation: The Pages Router has no direct equivalent. Developers typically use React Suspense or custom loading state variables.

questions.question: How do you colocate tests with pages in Next.js without them being treated as routes?
options: Using the pageExtensions config to exclude test files
questions.explanation: You can configure pageExtensions to only pick up page.tsx files, or keep tests in __tests__ which Next.js ignores by default.

questions.question: What is the role of generateStaticParams() in App Router?
options: Statically generates dynamic route segments at build time
questions.explanation: generateStaticParams() replaces getStaticPaths and tells Next.js which dynamic segments to statically generate at build time.

questions.question: What caching mechanism does Next.js use for fetch() requests in Server Components?
options: Extended fetch cache with { next: { revalidate } } options
questions.explanation: Next.js extends native fetch with { cache, next: { revalidate, tags } } options for fine-grained server-side caching.

questions.question: What does unstable_noStore() do?
options: Opts a fetch call or component out of static caching (equivalent to cache: 'no-store')
Removes data from the router cache
questions.explanation: unstable_noStore() marks a component or fetch as dynamic, preventing any caching of that data.

questions.question: What is the default port for next dev?
questions.explanation: Next.js development server starts on port 3000 by default. Use -p flag to change it.

questions.question: Which runtime does Middleware run on by default?
questions.explanation: Middleware runs on the Edge Runtime by default for low-latency execution close to the user.

questions.question: What is the route group syntax in App Router?
questions.explanation: Folders wrapped in parentheses like (marketing)/ create route groups that organise routes without affecting the URL path.

questions.question: What does a route group achieve?
options: Groups routes for shared layout without changing the URL
questions.explanation: Route groups allow sharing layouts, loading states, and error boundaries among grouped routes without URL namespace pollution.

questions.question: Where do you handle global errors in the App Router?
questions.explanation: app/global-error.tsx catches errors in the root layout and must include <html> and <body> tags since it replaces the layout.

questions.question: What does the template.tsx file do differently from layout.tsx?
options: It is re-mounted on every navigation, creating fresh state each time
It is used for error pages only
questions.explanation: template.tsx creates a new instance on each navigation (re-mounts), useful for enter/exit animations or resetting state.

questions.question: How do you share state between Server and Client Components?
options: Via props, URL search params, cookies, or server context
questions.explanation: Since RSCs can't use React state, shared state flows through props, URL parameters, cookies, or React context provided by Client Components.

questions.question: What is the next/headers module used for?
options: Reading request headers and cookies in Server Components and Route Handlers
questions.explanation: next/headers exports headers() and cookies() functions to read incoming request data from Server Components and Route Handlers.

questions.question: How do you add custom HTTP response headers to all pages?
options: Using the headers() function in next.config.js
questions.explanation: next.config.js exports an async headers() function returning header rules applied to matching routes at the CDN/server level.

questions.question: What are Streaming and Suspense used for in Next.js?
options: Progressively sending UI to the browser as server data resolves
questions.explanation: Streaming sends HTML in chunks via Suspense boundaries, letting the browser render fast parts while slow data loads separately.

questions.question: What is the _app.tsx file used for in Pages Router?
options: Global layout, providers, and CSS imports
questions.explanation: _app.tsx wraps all pages, making it the right place for global state providers, persistent layouts, and global CSS.

questions.question: How do you add a custom Document in Pages Router?
questions.explanation: _document.tsx lets you customise the <html> and <body> tags, inject scripts, and configure the server-side HTML shell.

questions.question: What does 'next start' do?
options: Serves a production build created by next build
questions.explanation: next start runs the production server. You must run next build first to generate the .next directory.

questions.question: How do you prefetch a Link in Next.js?
options: It prefetches automatically when the link enters the viewport (in production)
questions.explanation: By default, <Link> prefetches the linked page in the background when it becomes visible in the viewport during production.

questions.question: What is the useSearchParams() hook used for?
options: Reading and updating the URL path
Reading URL query string parameters on the client
questions.explanation: useSearchParams() reads the current URL's query string as a URLSearchParams object in Client Components.

questions.question: How do you update search params without a full navigation?
questions.explanation: router.push() or router.replace() with updated URLSearchParams updates the URL and triggers a soft navigation.

questions.question: What does the Next.js Image component's 'fill' prop do?
options: Makes the image cover the full page
Fills the nearest positioned parent container
questions.explanation: fill causes the image to expand to cover its nearest positioned ancestor, replacing explicit width/height props.

questions.question: What is required when using next/image with an external URL?
options: Adding the domain to images.remotePatterns in next.config.js
questions.explanation: External image URLs must be explicitly allowed via images.remotePatterns (or deprecated images.domains) in next.config.js.

questions.question: What does 'cache: no-store' do in a Server Component fetch call?
options: Forces the fetch to run on every request, disabling any caching
questions.explanation: cache: 'no-store' makes the fetch always run fresh on every request, equivalent to opting into dynamic rendering.

questions.question: Which Next.js feature lets you run code closer to the user globally?
questions.explanation: The Edge Runtime executes code at CDN edge nodes worldwide, reducing latency for geographically distributed users.

questions.question: How do you export the Edge runtime for a route?
questions.explanation: Adding export const runtime = 'edge' to a route file or layout opts it into the Edge Runtime.

questions.question: What is next-intl used for?
questions.explanation: next-intl is a popular library providing i18n routing, locale detection, and typed translations for Next.js.

questions.question: What does the 'cookies()' function from next/headers return?
options: A read-only interface to the request cookies in Server Components
questions.explanation: cookies() in Server Components is read-only. To set cookies you use cookies().set() in Route Handlers or Server Actions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a catch-all route segment [...slug]?
options: Matches one or more dynamic path segments
questions.explanation: [...slug] creates a catch-all segment that matches /a, /a/b, /a/b/c, returning all segments as an array.

questions.question: How does [[...slug]] differ from [...slug]?
options: [[...slug]] is also optional, matching the parent path with no segments
questions.explanation: [[...slug]] is an optional catch-all: it also matches the route with no segment at all (e.g., /), while [...slug] requires at least one segment.

questions.question: What happens if you export multiple default components from page.tsx?
options: Build error — only one default export is allowed
questions.explanation: A page.tsx must export exactly one React component as the default export; multiple defaults cause a build error.

questions.question: What is the 'shallow' routing option in Pages Router?
options: Updates the URL without running data fetching methods
A deprecated feature replaced by partial rendering
questions.explanation: { shallow: true } in router.push() changes the URL and updates query params without re-running getServerSideProps/getStaticProps.

questions.question: How do you add Google Analytics to a Next.js app efficiently?
options: Import GA library in every component
questions.explanation: next/script with strategy='afterInteractive' defers the script until the page is interactive, avoiding performance impact.

questions.question: What does 'strategy=beforeInteractive' do in next/script?
options: Loads the script after the page is interactive
Injects the script in the server-rendered HTML, blocking until loaded
Schedules the script for the next frame
questions.explanation: beforeInteractive injects the script into the server-rendered HTML so it loads and executes before hydration — use sparingly for critical scripts.

questions.question: What is draft mode in Next.js?
options: A way to preview unpublished CMS content by bypassing static generation
questions.explanation: Draft Mode lets you preview unpublished CMS content by temporarily opting out of static rendering via a secure cookie.

questions.question: Which metadata approach is used in the App Router?
options: Exporting a metadata object or generateMetadata() from layout/page files
questions.explanation: App Router uses a Metadata API — export const metadata = {...} or async generateMetadata() — for SEO, OG tags, and more.

questions.question: How do you generate dynamic OG images in Next.js?
options: Using ImageResponse from next/og in a Route Handler
questions.explanation: next/og provides ImageResponse which uses JSX and Satori to generate OG images dynamically on the Edge.

questions.question: What is the purpose of generateViewport() in App Router?
options: Sets the viewport meta tag dynamically per page
Configures the window size for SSR
questions.explanation: generateViewport() (or export const viewport) sets the viewport meta tag, supporting dynamic values based on route params.

questions.question: What is 'PPR' (Partial Pre-Rendering) in Next.js?
options: Pre-renders only the first 50% of a page
A rendering model combining static shells with dynamic streaming holes in a single request
A build cache for unchanged pages
questions.explanation: PPR (experimental) serves a static HTML shell instantly and streams dynamic content into Suspense boundaries in the same HTTP response.

questions.question: Where does app/favicon.ico go in the App Router?
options: Directly in the /app directory as a special file
questions.explanation: Placing favicon.ico (and other metadata files like apple-icon, opengraph-image) in /app gives them special handling by Next.js.

questions.question: What is next/form used for?
options: A <Form> component that pairs with Server Actions for progressive enhancement
questions.explanation: next/form provides a Form component that integrates with Server Actions, pre-fetches on focus, and works without JS.

questions.question: How do you revalidate data by tag in Next.js?
options: revalidateTag(tag) after tagging fetches with { next: { tags: ['tag'] } }
questions.explanation: Tag fetches with { next: { tags } } then call revalidateTag() to invalidate all cached data sharing that tag.

questions.question: What does 'use server' do at the top of a file?
options: Marks every export as a Server Action
Marks the file as a server-only module
questions.explanation: 'use server' at file scope marks all exports as Server Actions and also ensures the file only runs on the server.

questions.question: What triggers a full reload vs a soft navigation in App Router?
options: Hard navigation reloads the page; <Link> and router methods do a soft navigation preserving client state
Both methods always do a hard reload
Soft navigations only work with route groups
questions.explanation: Next.js <Link> and router.push() do soft navigations, only fetching changed segments. window.location causes full reloads.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to fetch data in Server Components?
options: Direct async/await inside the component function
questions.explanation: Server Components can be async functions, so you can directly await fetch() or database calls at the top level.

questions.question: How do you pass server data to a Client Component?
options: Via props from the Server Component parent
questions.explanation: A Server Component fetches the data and passes it as props to the Client Component. Props must be serialisable.

questions.question: What library does Next.js use internally for its router cache?
questions.explanation: Next.js uses React's cache() function to deduplicate data fetches within a single render pass on the server.

questions.question: Which version introduced the App Router as stable?
questions.explanation: The App Router was marked stable in Next.js 13.4 (May 2023) after being introduced as experimental in 13.0.

questions.question: How do you create a sitemap in App Router?
options: Export a sitemap() function from app/sitemap.ts
questions.explanation: app/sitemap.ts exports a default function returning a SitemapEntry array that Next.js auto-serves at /sitemap.xml.

questions.question: What is the default cache behaviour of Router Cache in App Router?
options: Routes are cached in the browser for the session
Routes are cached for 60 seconds only
questions.explanation: The Router Cache stores prefetched and visited route segments in memory for the duration of the user's session.

questions.question: What is next/og's ImageResponse built on?
questions.explanation: ImageResponse uses Satori to convert JSX into SVG then to PNG/JPEG, designed to run on the lightweight Edge Runtime.

questions.question: How do you create an optional catch-all route that also handles the parent path?
questions.explanation: [[...slug]] matches zero or more segments, including the parent route itself (/), unlike [...slug] which needs at least one.

questions.question: What does the 'permanentRedirect' function do in Server Components?
options: Same as redirect() but sets 308 status
questions.explanation: permanentRedirect() issues a 308 Permanent Redirect (vs redirect() which issues 307/303), telling crawlers the URL has moved permanently.

questions.question: In App Router, what component must wrap useSearchParams() in a Server Component context?
questions.explanation: useSearchParams() opts the component into dynamic rendering, requiring a Suspense boundary to avoid suspending the entire page.

questions.question: How do you suppress Next.js hydration warnings for intentional mismatches?
questions.explanation: The suppressHydrationWarning prop on an HTML element tells React to ignore intentional server/client mismatches like timestamps.

questions.question: What is dynamic() from next/dynamic used for?
options: Lazy-loading components with optional SSR disable and loading fallbacks
questions.explanation: next/dynamic wraps React.lazy with SSR support, optional { ssr: false } to skip server rendering, and loading fallback.

questions.question: What does ssr: false in next/dynamic do?
options: Disables SSR for the whole page
Prevents the dynamic component from rendering on the server
questions.explanation: { ssr: false } defers component rendering to the client only — useful for browser-only libraries like chart.js or mapbox.

questions.question: Which directory serves static assets like images and robots.txt?
questions.explanation: Files in /public are served at the root URL. /public/robots.txt is accessible at /robots.txt.

questions.question: How do you add TypeScript to an existing Next.js project?
options: Create tsconfig.json — Next.js auto-configures it on next dev
questions.explanation: Creating an empty tsconfig.json triggers Next.js to auto-populate it with correct TypeScript settings on the next build/dev.

questions.question: What is the 'standalone' output mode in next.config.js?
options: Produces a minimal server bundle that only includes necessary files for deployment
questions.explanation: output: 'standalone' creates a self-contained deployment artifact (great for Docker) by tracing only the required node_modules.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the instrumentation.ts file in Next.js?
options: Sets up observability tools (OpenTelemetry) that run when the server starts
questions.explanation: instrumentation.ts exports a register() function that Next.js calls once when the server initialises, used for tracing/monitoring setup.

questions.question: How does Next.js handle CSS Modules?
options: CSS files ending in .module.css are scoped automatically
questions.explanation: Any file named *.module.css is treated as a CSS Module — class names are locally scoped to prevent conflicts.

questions.question: What does Tailwind CSS require to work with Next.js?
options: Install tailwindcss, run npx tailwindcss init, configure content paths, import in globals.css
It works out of the box
questions.explanation: Install tailwindcss + postcss + autoprefixer, create tailwind.config.js with content paths, and import Tailwind directives in your global CSS.

questions.question: What is the App Router's equivalent of getInitialProps?
options: Direct async data fetching in Server Components
questions.explanation: getInitialProps was a Pages Router pattern. In App Router you just use async Server Components or generateMetadata() for layout data.

questions.question: How do you access route params in a Server Component page?
options: Via the params prop passed by Next.js to the page component
questions.explanation: In App Router, page and layout components automatically receive a params prop containing the dynamic segment values.

questions.question: Which of these correctly imports the Link component?
questions.explanation: The Link component is a default export from 'next/link'. Don't confuse it with hooks in 'next/navigation'.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of React Server Components over traditional SSR?
options: They never send component code to the client, reducing JS bundle size
questions.explanation: RSC code stays on the server entirely — the client receives the rendered output, not the JavaScript, shrinking the client bundle.

questions.question: What happens to unused JavaScript in a Server Component subtree?
options: It is never sent to the client at all
It is inlined as a script tag
questions.explanation: Since RSCs run only on the server, their import chain is never included in the client JS bundle.

questions.question: How do you opt into Node.js runtime (not Edge) for a specific route?
options: runtime: 'nodejs' in next.config.js for the route
It is the default for App Router routes
questions.explanation: export const runtime = 'nodejs' explicitly sets the route to run in the Node.js runtime with full Node APIs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the unstable_cache() function?
options: Caches any async function result with a key and optional revalidation
questions.explanation: unstable_cache() wraps any async function (e.g. DB queries) with persistent caching, tags, and revalidation — like fetch() cache for non-fetch data.

questions.question: How does Next.js support absolute imports?
questions.explanation: Setting baseUrl (and optionally paths) in tsconfig.json enables absolute imports like 'components/Button' instead of '../../components/Button'.

questions.question: What does the 'forbidden()' function do in App Router?
questions.explanation: Calling forbidden() throws a 403 Forbidden response, rendering the nearest forbidden.tsx error UI.

questions.question: What is the experimental 'after()' API in Next.js 15?
options: Schedules work to run after the response is sent
questions.explanation: after() (stable in Next.js 15) lets you schedule non-critical tasks (logging, analytics) to run after the response has been streamed.

questions.question: What change did Next.js 15 make to fetch caching defaults?
options: All fetches are now cached by default
Fetches are now uncached (no-store) by default; you opt INTO caching
questions.explanation: Next.js 15 reversed the default: fetch requests are no longer cached by default. Add { cache: 'force-cache' } to opt in.

topics.name: Node.js
topics.description: Async JavaScript runtime — event loop, streams, modules, and APIs

questions.question: What JavaScript engine does Node.js use?
questions.explanation: Node.js is built on Google's V8 engine (also used in Chrome), which compiles JS to native machine code.

questions.question: What is the Event Loop in Node.js?
options: A mechanism that offloads I/O operations and executes callbacks when they complete
A for-loop that processes events synchronously
questions.explanation: The Event Loop lets Node.js perform non-blocking I/O by delegating operations to the OS/libuv and picking up callbacks when they finish.

questions.question: Which module system does Node.js use by default?
questions.explanation: CommonJS is the default. Node.js also supports ES Modules via .mjs extension or "type": "module" in package.json.

questions.question: How do you use ES Modules in a Node.js project?
options: Set "type": "module" in package.json or use .mjs extension
questions.explanation: Setting "type": "module" makes all .js files in the package use ES Module syntax (import/export).

questions.question: What is libuv?
options: A JavaScript library for async patterns
A C library providing Node.js's event loop, thread pool, and async I/O
questions.explanation: libuv is the C library underneath Node.js that implements the event loop, thread pool (for file I/O, crypto, etc.), and cross-platform async I/O.

questions.question: How many threads does Node.js use for JavaScript execution by default?
options: Multiple threads equal to CPU cores
One main thread for JS execution
Two — one for sync, one for async
questions.explanation: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single main thread. The libuv thread pool handles I/O but JS itself is single-threaded.

questions.question: What is the default size of the libuv thread pool?
questions.explanation: The libuv thread pool defaults to 4 threads. Set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE env var to change it (max 1024).

questions.question: What does process.nextTick() do?
options: Schedules a callback after the next I/O event
Schedules a callback at the end of the current operation, before any I/O
questions.explanation: process.nextTick() queues a callback to run at the end of the current phase, before the event loop moves on — even before Promise microtasks.

questions.question: What is the microtask queue in Node.js?
options: A queue for Promise resolutions and queueMicrotask() callbacks, processed before each event loop phase
questions.explanation: Microtasks (Promise .then, queueMicrotask) drain completely after each C++ -> JS transition before the event loop continues.

questions.question: What is the order of event loop phases?
options: timers → I/O callbacks → idle → poll → check → close callbacks
questions.explanation: The phases are: timers (setTimeout/setInterval), pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll (fetch I/O), check (setImmediate), close callbacks.

questions.question: What does setImmediate() do?
options: Queues a callback in the check phase, after I/O events
questions.explanation: setImmediate() fires in the check phase of the event loop, always after I/O callbacks in the current iteration.

questions.question: What is the difference between setImmediate() and setTimeout(fn, 0)?
options: setImmediate runs in the check phase; setTimeout(fn,0) runs in the timers phase — order depends on context
questions.explanation: When called outside I/O, their order is non-deterministic. Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always fires before setTimeout(fn,0).

questions.question: How do you read a file asynchronously in Node.js?
questions.explanation: fs.readFile() is the standard async file read, accepting a path, optional encoding, and a callback(err, data).

questions.question: What does fs.readFileSync() do differently?
options: It blocks the event loop until the file is read
questions.explanation: readFileSync blocks the entire Node.js process until the file is fully read — fine for startup, harmful in request handlers.

questions.question: What is a Stream in Node.js?
options: A real-time data channel to a database
An abstract interface for working with streaming data — data processed in chunks
questions.explanation: Streams process data piece by piece, enabling memory-efficient handling of large files, network data, and more.

questions.question: What are the four types of streams in Node.js?
questions.explanation: Readable (source), Writable (destination), Duplex (both), Transform (duplex that modifies data) are the four stream types.

questions.question: What does stream.pipe() do?
options: Pipes the output of a Readable stream into a Writable stream automatically
questions.explanation: pipe() handles the data, pause, resume, and end events automatically, forwarding chunks from readable to writable.

questions.question: What is the 'http' module used for?
options: Creating HTTP servers and making HTTP client requests
questions.explanation: Node.js's built-in 'http' module lets you create servers (http.createServer) and make client requests (http.request/get).

questions.question: How do you create a simple HTTP server in Node.js?
questions.explanation: http.createServer() accepts a request listener function and .listen() binds it to a port.

questions.question: What is the 'path' module used for?
options: File path manipulation (join, resolve, extname, basename, etc.)
questions.explanation: The built-in 'path' module provides cross-platform file path utilities, handling Windows backslashes vs POSIX forward slashes.

questions.question: What does path.join() do?
options: Joins path segments using the OS separator and normalises the result
questions.explanation: path.join() combines segments with the platform separator and cleans up double slashes and . / .. references.

questions.question: What is __dirname in Node.js?
options: The absolute path of the directory containing the current module file
questions.explanation: __dirname is a CommonJS global giving the absolute path to the folder where the current script lives.

questions.question: Is __dirname available in ES Modules?
options: No — use import.meta.url and fileURLToPath to replicate it
questions.explanation: ESM doesn't inject __dirname. Use: const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)).

questions.question: What is the 'os' module used for?
options: Accessing operating system information (CPUs, memory, platform, hostname)
questions.explanation: The 'os' module exposes os.cpus(), os.freemem(), os.platform(), os.homedir(), and more.

questions.question: What does process.env do?
options: Provides access to all environment variables as key-value strings
questions.explanation: process.env is an object containing all environment variables inherited by the process — used for config, secrets, feature flags.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'events' module?
options: Provides the EventEmitter class for building event-driven architectures
questions.explanation: EventEmitter is the backbone of Node.js's event system. Stream, http.Server, process, and most core classes extend it.

questions.question: How do you emit a custom event with EventEmitter?
questions.explanation: emitter.emit('eventName', ...args) triggers all listeners registered with .on('eventName', cb).

questions.question: What does the 'crypto' module provide?
options: Cryptographic functions: hashing, HMAC, encryption, key generation
questions.explanation: Node.js's built-in 'crypto' module wraps OpenSSL and provides hash (SHA-256 etc.), HMAC, AES, RSA, and random byte generation.

questions.question: How do you hash a password safely in Node.js?
questions.explanation: Use bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt for passwords — they are slow by design. MD5 and SHA-256 are fast and unsuitable for passwords.

questions.question: What is a Buffer in Node.js?
options: A fixed-size chunk of raw binary memory outside V8's heap
questions.explanation: Buffer represents raw binary data. It is used for I/O operations, binary protocols, and working with streams.

questions.question: How do you create a Buffer from a string?
questions.explanation: Buffer.from() is the preferred constructor. new Buffer() is deprecated. The second arg specifies encoding (default utf8).

questions.question: What does npm init -y do?
options: Creates a package.json with default values without prompts
questions.explanation: -y (or --yes) skips the interactive prompt and creates package.json with defaults.

questions.question: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
options: dependencies are needed at runtime; devDependencies are only needed during development/build
questions.explanation: dependencies ship with production builds; devDependencies (testing, linting, bundlers) aren't installed when NODE_ENV=production.

questions.question: What does npm install --save-dev do?
options: Installs a package and adds it to devDependencies
questions.explanation: --save-dev (or -D) adds the package to devDependencies in package.json, for build-time tools.

questions.question: What is package-lock.json for?
options: Recording the exact versions of every installed dependency for reproducible installs
questions.explanation: package-lock.json captures the exact resolved versions and source hashes so every install produces identical node_modules.

questions.question: What is the 'cluster' module used for?
options: Spawning multiple Node.js worker processes to use all CPU cores
questions.explanation: cluster forks child processes sharing the same server port, allowing Node.js to utilise multi-core machines.

questions.question: What are Worker Threads?
options: A way to run JavaScript in parallel threads within the same process
questions.explanation: worker_threads allow CPU-intensive JS to run in parallel without blocking the main thread, sharing memory via SharedArrayBuffer.

questions.question: When should you use Worker Threads vs cluster?
options: Worker Threads for CPU-bound tasks sharing data; cluster for scaling a server across CPU cores
questions.explanation: Use worker_threads for parallel computation (image processing, crypto). Use cluster to scale an HTTP server across cores.

questions.question: How do you handle uncaught exceptions in Node.js?
options: process.on('uncaughtException', cb) — but restart the process after logging
It crashes automatically and that's best practice
questions.explanation: uncaughtException lets you log/alert before exiting, but the process should always restart (via PM2/nodemon) since state is undefined.

questions.question: What is the 'child_process' module used for?
options: Spawning subprocesses and running shell commands from Node.js
questions.explanation: child_process (spawn, exec, fork) creates child processes to run shell commands, other programs, or separate Node scripts.

questions.question: What is the difference between exec() and spawn() in child_process?
options: exec() buffers the entire output; spawn() streams stdout/stderr
spawn() is synchronous; exec() is async
questions.explanation: exec() collects all output then returns in a callback — bad for large output. spawn() streams stdout/stderr as they arrive.

questions.question: What does 'require.resolve()' do?
options: Returns the file path that would be loaded by require(), without actually loading it
questions.explanation: require.resolve() runs Node's module resolution algorithm and returns the resolved path — useful for finding module locations.

questions.question: What is the 'util' module's promisify function?
options: Wraps a callback-based function to return a Promise
questions.explanation: util.promisify(fn) takes a function following the (err, value) callback convention and returns a Promise-based version.

questions.question: What is Express.js?
options: A minimal and flexible Node.js web application framework
questions.explanation: Express is the most popular Node.js web framework, providing routing, middleware, and HTTP utilities with minimal overhead.

questions.question: How do you define a GET route in Express?
questions.explanation: app.get() registers a handler for GET requests to a specific path. Similar methods exist for POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.

questions.question: What is middleware in Express?
options: Functions that have access to req, res, and next — forming a processing pipeline
questions.explanation: Middleware functions run in order for each request. They can modify req/res, end the request, or call next() to pass to the next handler.

questions.question: How do you handle errors in Express middleware?
options: Define a middleware with four arguments: (err, req, res, next)
questions.explanation: Express identifies error-handling middleware by its 4-parameter signature (err, req, res, next) and routes errors there via next(err).

questions.question: What does CORS stand for and why is it relevant?
options: Client-Origin Resource Sharing — a Node.js security module
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — a browser policy preventing requests to different origins
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser security mechanism. Node.js servers must send appropriate headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin) to allow cross-origin requests.

questions.question: How do you parse JSON request bodies in Express?
questions.explanation: express.json() middleware (built-in since Express 4.16) parses incoming JSON payloads and populates req.body.

questions.question: What is the 'net' module used for?
options: Creating raw TCP/IPC servers and clients
questions.explanation: The 'net' module provides a TCP socket API — the foundation for HTTP, HTTPS, and custom protocols.

questions.question: What does 'pipe' do in a Transform stream?
options: Chains transformation logic between a Readable source and Writable destination
questions.explanation: Transform streams sit in the middle of a pipeline: data flows from Readable → Transform (modify) → Writable via pipe.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'url' module?
questions.explanation: Node.js's 'url' module provides the WHATWG URL API (new URL()) and legacy url.parse() for parsing/constructing URLs.

questions.question: How do you parse query string parameters in Node.js without Express?
questions.explanation: new URLSearchParams() is the modern WHATWG standard. The legacy querystring module is deprecated in favour of URLSearchParams.

questions.question: What is the 'dns' module used for?
options: Performing DNS lookups (resolve, lookup, reverse) from Node.js
questions.explanation: The 'dns' module provides dns.resolve(), dns.lookup() and other functions to query DNS servers from Node.js code.

questions.question: What is PM2?
options: A production process manager for Node.js with clustering, auto-restart, and log management
questions.explanation: PM2 is the standard production process manager for Node.js apps, handling restarts on crash, cluster mode, and built-in monitoring.

questions.question: What does 'node --inspect' do?
options: Enables the V8 Inspector for debugging with Chrome DevTools or VS Code
questions.explanation: --inspect opens a debugging port (default 9229) so you can attach DevTools or an IDE debugger for breakpoints and profiling.

questions.question: What is the difference between a readable stream in flowing vs paused mode?
options: Flowing: data events fire automatically; Paused: data must be pulled via stream.read()
Flowing is only for large files
questions.explanation: Paused mode gives backpressure control; flowing mode pushes data as fast as possible. Pipe handles this automatically.

questions.question: What is backpressure in Node.js streams?
options: CPU pressure from too many processes
When a writable stream can't keep up with a readable — signalling the readable to pause
questions.explanation: Backpressure prevents memory overflow by pausing the readable when writable.write() returns false, and resuming on 'drain'.

questions.question: How do you run a Node.js script?
questions.explanation: node <filename> executes the file. node run is not a command — that's npm run for scripts in package.json.

questions.question: What does 'nodemon' do?
options: Automatically restarts the Node.js application when file changes are detected
questions.explanation: nodemon watches the file system and restarts your app on save — essential for development.

questions.question: What is the purpose of '.env' files in Node.js projects?
options: Storing environment-specific configuration variables that shouldn't be in source code
questions.explanation: .env files (loaded via dotenv or Node.js 20.6's --env-file) store API keys, DB URLs, and other config outside version control.

questions.question: What does 'npm audit' do?
options: Checks installed packages for known security vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: npm audit compares your dependency tree against the npm advisory database and reports known CVEs.

questions.question: What is the Node.js REPL?
options: Read-Eval-Print Loop — an interactive shell for running JS expressions
questions.explanation: Running 'node' without arguments starts the REPL where you can evaluate JS expressions, inspect objects, and test code snippets.

questions.question: What is 'async_hooks' module used for?
options: Tracking the lifecycle of asynchronous resources for request-scoped context (e.g. AsyncLocalStorage)
questions.explanation: async_hooks enables AsyncLocalStorage which stores request-scoped data (like request IDs, user context) across async operations.

questions.question: What is AsyncLocalStorage used for?
options: Propagating context (e.g. request ID, user) through the async call chain without passing it explicitly
questions.explanation: AsyncLocalStorage creates a context that flows through all async operations within a store.run() call — like thread-local storage.

questions.question: How does Node.js handle HTTPS?
options: Via the 'https' module with TLS certificates
questions.explanation: The 'https' module creates HTTPS servers using TLS certificates (key, cert options). Production usually terminates TLS at a reverse proxy.

questions.question: What is the 'zlib' module for?
options: Compression and decompression (gzip, deflate, brotli) for HTTP responses and streams
questions.explanation: zlib provides streaming compression (createGzip, createBrotliCompress) used to compress HTTP responses or compress files.

questions.question: What is 'global' in Node.js?
options: The global namespace object, equivalent to 'window' in browsers
questions.explanation: global is the top-level object in Node.js. Variables set on it are accessible everywhere (avoid this pattern in favour of modules).

questions.question: What Node.js version introduced native ESM support without a flag?
questions.explanation: ESM support landed experimentally in Node.js 12 and became stable in Node.js 14, usable without a flag.

questions.question: What does the '--experimental-vm-modules' flag enable?
options: Running ES Modules in the vm module (needed for Jest's ESM support)
questions.explanation: This flag enables the vm.Module API, allowing Jest and other tools to run ESM code in isolated contexts.

questions.question: How do you check the installed Node.js version?
questions.explanation: node -v (or node --version) prints the current Node.js version number.

questions.question: What is 'nvm' used for?
options: Node Version Manager — switches between multiple Node.js versions on one machine
questions.explanation: nvm (or fnm, volta) lets developers install and switch between Node.js versions, important for projects with different requirements.

questions.question: What does 'npm ci' do differently from 'npm install'?
options: Uses package-lock.json exclusively, fails on version mismatches, for clean CI environments
questions.explanation: npm ci is optimised for CI: it deletes node_modules, installs exactly what's in package-lock.json, and fails if the lock file is out of sync.

questions.question: How do you publish a package to npm?
options: npm publish (after npm login and correct package.json)
questions.explanation: npm publish sends the package to the npm registry. The package must have a unique name in package.json and you must be logged in.

questions.question: What is the 'tls' module used for?
options: Creating TLS/SSL servers and clients at a lower level than 'https'
questions.explanation: The 'tls' module provides the low-level TLS socket API. The 'https' module uses it internally.

questions.question: What does 'process.exit(1)' do?
options: Terminates the process with exit code 1 (indicating an error)
questions.explanation: process.exit(code) immediately terminates Node.js. Exit code 0 = success; non-zero = error (used by shells/CI).

questions.question: What is the '--max-old-space-size' Node.js flag for?
options: Increasing the V8 heap memory limit (e.g. --max-old-space-size=4096 for 4GB)
questions.explanation: V8 defaults to ~1.5GB. Set --max-old-space-size=SIZE_MB to allow more heap memory for memory-intensive applications.

questions.question: What is Fastify?
options: A high-performance Node.js web framework with schema-based validation and a plugin system
questions.explanation: Fastify is one of the fastest Node.js web frameworks, using JSON schema validation (via ajv) for serialisation and input validation.

questions.question: How do you create a readable stream from a string in Node.js?
questions.explanation: Readable.from() creates a Readable from an iterable, async iterable, or any value — convenient for testing.

questions.question: What does 'fs.watch()' do?
options: Watches a file or directory for changes and fires a callback
questions.explanation: fs.watch() uses OS-level file watching (inotify/FSEvents) to notify on file/directory changes — used by nodemon, webpack, etc.

questions.question: What is the 'perf_hooks' module used for?
options: High-resolution timing (performance.now, PerformanceObserver) for profiling Node.js code
questions.explanation: perf_hooks exposes the Performance Timeline API in Node.js for precise timing, marks, measures, and HTTP timing.

questions.question: What does process.hrtime.bigint() return?
options: Current time in nanoseconds as a BigInt — for high-resolution benchmarks
questions.explanation: hrtime.bigint() returns nanosecond-precision monotonic time as BigInt, ideal for microbenchmarks.

questions.question: What is the module cache in Node.js?
options: require() caches loaded modules so subsequent require() calls return the cached export
A filesystem cache of transpiled files
questions.explanation: After the first require(), the module object is stored in require.cache. Subsequent requires return the same instance — the basis of singletons.

questions.question: How do you clear a cached module to force re-evaluation?
questions.explanation: Deleting the entry from require.cache causes the next require() call to re-execute and re-cache the module.

questions.question: What is the V8 flag '--expose-gc' used for?
options: Makes gc() function available in JS to manually trigger garbage collection (for testing/profiling)
questions.explanation: --expose-gc injects a global gc() function, useful for testing memory management or forcing collection in benchmarks.

questions.question: What are Node.js Diagnostic Reports?
options: JSON snapshots of the process state (heap, event loop, libuv handles) triggered on crash or signal
questions.explanation: Diagnostic reports (--report-on-signal, process.report.writeReport()) capture comprehensive snapshots for post-mortem debugging.

questions.question: What is the 'readline' module used for?
options: Reading files line by line only
Reading input line by line from any Readable stream, including stdin (CLI prompts)
questions.explanation: readline wraps any stream to emit 'line' events, used for interactive CLI tools, processing large text files, and parsing CSV.

questions.question: What does 'import.meta.url' give you in an ESM module?
options: The fully-qualified file:// URL of the current module file
questions.explanation: import.meta.url is the ESM equivalent of __filename — use with new URL() and fileURLToPath() to get directory paths.

questions.question: How do you detect if code is running in a Worker Thread?
questions.explanation: worker_threads.isMainThread is false when code is executing inside a Worker Thread.

questions.question: What is the purpose of SharedArrayBuffer in Worker Threads?
options: Allows multiple worker threads to share the same memory region directly without copying
questions.explanation: SharedArrayBuffer lets Worker Threads share raw memory, enabling high-performance parallel computation via Atomics operations.

questions.question: What is the 'trace_events' module for?
options: Enabling V8, Node.js core, and user-space trace events for performance profiling via chrome://tracing
questions.explanation: trace_events produces a trace log compatible with Chrome's tracing format for deep performance analysis.

questions.question: What does '--require module' flag do when starting Node.js?
options: Pre-loads a CommonJS module before executing the entry file
questions.explanation: --require (or -r) preloads a module, useful for loading dotenv, ts-node/register, or instrumentation before your app starts.

questions.question: What HTTP/2 support does Node.js have?
options: Built-in via the 'http2' module with full multiplexing and server push support
questions.explanation: Node.js includes a full HTTP/2 implementation via 'http2' module supporting streams, multiplexing, headers compression, and server push.

questions.question: What is the 'vm' module used for?
options: Running JavaScript code in a sandboxed V8 context
questions.explanation: vm.runInNewContext() executes code in an isolated V8 context with its own global. Used for sandboxing, testing, and template engines.

topics.name: Docker
topics.description: Container platform — images, Dockerfiles, Compose, and networking

questions.question: What is Docker?
options: A platform for building, shipping, and running applications in lightweight containers
questions.explanation: Docker packages applications and their dependencies into containers — isolated, portable, and consistent across environments.

questions.question: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
options: Containers share the host OS kernel and are lightweight; VMs include a full OS and are heavier
questions.explanation: Containers virtualise at the OS process level (shared kernel) making them far lighter than VMs which emulate full hardware.

questions.question: What is a Docker image?
options: A read-only template with layers defining an application's filesystem and config
questions.explanation: Images are immutable layer stacks used to create containers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile adds a layer.

questions.question: What command runs a container from an image?
questions.explanation: docker run creates and starts a container from an image. Use docker start to restart a stopped container.

questions.question: What does the '-d' flag do in 'docker run -d'?
options: Detached mode — runs the container in the background
questions.explanation: -d (detached) starts the container in the background, returning the container ID without attaching to its output.

questions.question: What is a Dockerfile?
options: A text file with instructions to build a Docker image
questions.explanation: A Dockerfile contains ordered instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, etc.) that Docker executes to build an image.

questions.question: What does the FROM instruction do in a Dockerfile?
options: Specifies the base image to build from
questions.explanation: FROM sets the starting point. Every Dockerfile must start with FROM (or ARG before FROM for build args).

questions.question: What is the difference between RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT?
options: RUN executes at build time; CMD/ENTRYPOINT define the default command at container start
CMD runs at build; RUN at start
questions.explanation: RUN adds image layers during build. CMD provides default arguments; ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable. CMD args are passed to ENTRYPOINT.

questions.question: What does COPY vs ADD do in a Dockerfile?
options: COPY copies local files; ADD also supports URLs and auto-extracts tar archives
questions.explanation: Prefer COPY for local file copies. ADD's extra features (URL, tar extraction) can cause unexpected behaviour.

questions.question: What is a multi-stage build in Docker?
options: Using multiple FROM stages to produce a lean final image, discarding build dependencies
Running multiple containers in one build
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds compile in one stage (with full toolchain), then COPY only the artifact into a minimal final image.

questions.question: How do you build an image from a Dockerfile?
questions.explanation: docker build -t name:tag . builds an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory and tags it.

questions.question: What is Docker Hub?
options: A public/private registry for storing and sharing Docker images
questions.explanation: Docker Hub is the default public image registry. docker push/pull use it unless a different registry is specified.

questions.question: How do you list running containers?
questions.explanation: docker ps lists running containers. docker ps -a includes stopped containers.

questions.question: How do you stop a running container?
questions.explanation: docker stop sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after a grace period. docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately.

questions.question: How do you remove a container?
questions.explanation: docker rm removes a stopped container. Use docker rm -f to force-remove a running container.

questions.question: What is a Docker Volume?
options: Persistent storage managed by Docker, surviving container restarts and removal
questions.explanation: Volumes store data outside the container's writable layer, persisting across container recreations.

questions.question: What is a bind mount?
options: Mapping a host directory directly into a container
questions.explanation: Bind mounts (--mount type=bind,src=/host/path,dst=/container/path) reflect host filesystem changes immediately in the container.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose?
options: A tool for defining and running multi-container apps with a YAML config file
questions.explanation: docker-compose (or docker compose) reads docker-compose.yml to spin up entire application stacks with one command.

questions.question: What command starts all services in a docker-compose.yml?
questions.explanation: docker compose up (or docker-compose up) starts all services. Add -d for detached mode.

questions.question: What does 'docker compose down' do?
options: Stops and removes containers, networks created by compose up
questions.explanation: compose down stops and removes containers and networks. Add --volumes to also remove named volumes.

questions.question: What is the default Docker network type?
questions.explanation: The default network driver is 'bridge' — containers get a virtual network interface connected to a virtual bridge on the host.

questions.question: What is the 'host' network mode?
options: Routes traffic through the host's firewall
Removes network isolation — the container shares the host's network stack directly
questions.explanation: Host network mode eliminates the NAT layer; the container's port IS the host's port. Only available on Linux Docker.

questions.question: How do you expose a container port to the host?
options: Both A and B, but B is required to actually map it
questions.explanation: EXPOSE documents the port; -p actually maps it to the host. EXPOSE alone does nothing unless you run docker run -P.

questions.question: What does '-P' (uppercase) do in docker run?
options: Maps all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports
questions.explanation: docker run -P automatically maps every EXPOSE'd port to a random ephemeral port on the host.

questions.question: What is a Docker overlay network?
options: A multi-host network spanning Docker nodes in a Swarm cluster
questions.explanation: Overlay networks connect containers across multiple Docker hosts (Swarm nodes) using VXLAN tunnelling.

questions.question: What is the .dockerignore file used for?
options: Excluding files/dirs from the build context sent to the Docker daemon
questions.explanation: .dockerignore works like .gitignore — exclude node_modules, .git, .env etc. to speed up builds and reduce context size.

questions.question: How do you pass environment variables to a container?
options: docker run -e KEY=VALUE or via docker-compose environment section
questions.explanation: -e KEY=VALUE (or --env-file .env) injects env vars at runtime. ENV in Dockerfile sets build-time defaults.

questions.question: What is Docker Swarm?
options: Docker's built-in container orchestration for clustering and service management
questions.explanation: Docker Swarm turns multiple Docker hosts into a cluster with services, replicas, rolling updates, and load balancing.

questions.question: What is Kubernetes, and how does it relate to Docker?
options: A container orchestration platform that can run Docker containers at scale
questions.explanation: Kubernetes (K8s) is a production-grade orchestrator. It uses container runtimes (historically Docker, now containerd) to manage containers.

questions.question: What is the best practice for running containers as root?
options: Always run as root for simplicity
Avoid it — create a non-root USER in the Dockerfile for security
Root is required for all Node.js apps
questions.explanation: Running as root inside a container is a security risk. Use USER directive to run as a non-privileged user.

questions.question: What is image layer caching and why does it matter?
options: Docker reuses unchanged layers from previous builds, drastically speeding up rebuilds
A Dockerfile feature only available on Linux
questions.explanation: Instructions that haven't changed reuse cached layers. Order Dockerfile instructions least-to-most-changing to maximise cache hits.

questions.question: How do you view logs of a running container?
questions.explanation: docker logs shows stdout/stderr of a container. Add -f to follow (tail -f equivalent).

questions.question: How do you execute a command inside a running container?
questions.explanation: docker exec -it opens an interactive terminal inside an already-running container — useful for debugging.

questions.question: What does 'docker inspect' do?
options: Returns detailed JSON about a container, image, volume, or network
questions.explanation: docker inspect outputs low-level configuration and state as JSON — IP address, mounts, environment, network settings, etc.

questions.question: What is a Docker healthcheck?
options: A Dockerfile or run instruction that periodically tests if the container is healthy
A liveness probe for Kubernetes only
questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK in a Dockerfile or --health-cmd in docker run runs a command periodically; unhealthy containers can be restarted.

questions.question: What is the purpose of WORKDIR in a Dockerfile?
options: Sets the working directory on the host
Sets the working directory inside the image for subsequent instructions and the container
Mounts a volume at that path
questions.explanation: WORKDIR sets the cwd for RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, ADD. It creates the directory if it doesn't exist.

questions.question: What does 'docker system prune' do?
options: Removes all stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks, and build cache
questions.explanation: docker system prune frees up disk space by removing unused Docker objects. Add -a to also remove unused images.

questions.question: What is a dangling image?
options: An image with no tag (tag is <none>) — typically old build layers superseded by a new build
A pulled but never run image
questions.explanation: When you rebuild an image with the same tag, the old layers become untagged/dangling. Remove them with docker image prune.

questions.question: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
options: ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable; CMD provides default arguments that can be overridden at runtime
CMD is for Linux; ENTRYPOINT for Windows
Only one can be used per Dockerfile
questions.explanation: docker run image arg replaces CMD args but passes to ENTRYPOINT. Use ENTRYPOINT for the executable, CMD for default args.

questions.question: What is Docker BuildKit?
options: An improved build engine with parallel builds, better caching, and secret mounts
questions.explanation: BuildKit (default since Docker 23) enables concurrent layer builds, better cache management, secret mounts (--mount=type=secret), and SSH forwarding.

questions.question: How do you pass secrets securely during a Docker build without storing them in layers?
options: COPY the secret then delete it
questions.explanation: BuildKit secret mounts expose a secret file only during that RUN instruction — it never appears in the image layer.

questions.question: What is the purpose of ARG in a Dockerfile?
options: Defines build-time variables passed via --build-arg, not persisted in the final image (unless ENV'd)
questions.explanation: ARG values are only available during the build. Never use ARG for secrets — they appear in docker history.

questions.question: What does 'depends_on' do in docker-compose.yml?
options: Controls startup order — service waits until dependent containers are started (not necessarily healthy)
questions.explanation: depends_on ensures startup order but not readiness. Use healthchecks + condition: service_healthy for true dependency.

questions.question: What is the 'networks' key in docker-compose.yml used for?
options: Defining custom networks so services can communicate by service name
questions.explanation: Compose creates a default network so services resolve each other by name. Custom networks allow isolation between service groups.

questions.question: How do containers in the same Compose network communicate?
options: By service name as the hostname (DNS resolution within the Docker network)
questions.explanation: Docker's embedded DNS resolves container/service names to IPs within the same network — no hardcoded IPs needed.

questions.question: What is the recommended base image for a production Node.js Docker container?
questions.explanation: Alpine/slim variants are much smaller (< 100MB vs 1GB+ for full images), reducing attack surface and pull times.

questions.question: What does EXPOSE 3000 in a Dockerfile actually do?
options: Documents that the container listens on port 3000 — but does NOT publish it to the host
questions.explanation: EXPOSE is metadata/documentation only. You still need -p 3000:3000 in docker run to map it to the host.

questions.question: What is a multi-platform Docker image?
options: An image with multiple OS variants
A single image manifest that supports multiple CPU architectures (amd64, arm64, etc.)
An image deployed across multiple registries
A Compose config for multiple environments
questions.explanation: Multi-platform images (built with docker buildx) contain manifests for amd64, arm64, etc. Docker pulls the right variant automatically.

questions.question: What is 'docker buildx' used for?
options: Extended build capabilities: multi-platform builds, remote builders, and advanced caching
questions.explanation: docker buildx extends docker build with multi-platform support, remote builders, and better cache export/import.

questions.question: What is containerd?
options: An industry-standard container runtime that Docker and Kubernetes use under the hood
questions.explanation: containerd is the CNCF runtime that manages the container lifecycle. Docker Engine uses it internally; Kubernetes uses it directly.

questions.question: How do you tag a Docker image for a private registry?
questions.explanation: docker tag creates an alias with the registry prefix, then docker push sends it to that registry.

questions.question: What is the best way to reduce Docker image size?
options: Use a large base image with everything pre-installed
Multi-stage builds + minimal base image + merge RUN commands + use .dockerignore
questions.explanation: Combine RUN commands to reduce layers, use Alpine/scratch bases, copy only build artifacts via multi-stage, and exclude dev files.
